'''''Camassia quamash''''', commonly known as '''camas''', '''kwetlal''',<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Corntassel |first1=Jeff |author2=Cheryl Bryce |title=Practicing Sustainable Self-Determination: Indigenous Approaches to Cultural Restoration and Revitalization |journal=The Brown Journal of World Affairs |volume=18 |issue=2 |year=2012 |pages=151–162 |jstor=24590870 |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/24590870}}</ref> '''small camas''',<ref>{{PLANTS|symbol=CAQU2|taxon=Camassia quamash|accessdate=1 February 2013}}</ref> '''common camas''',<ref>{{cite book |last=Kozloff |first=Eugene N. |title=Plants of Western Oregon, Washington & British Columbia |year=2005 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |isbn=978-0-88192-724-5 |page=410}}</ref> '''common camash'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''quamash''', is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herb]]. It is [[Native plant|native]] to western [[North America]] in large areas of southern [[Canada]] and the northwestern [[United States]].

==Description==
''Camassia quamash'' is a [[perennial]] plant with a [[herbaceous]] character that has a wide range of variation across its geographical range.<ref name="FNA">{{cite web |last1=Ranker |first1= Tom A. |last2=Hogan |first2=Tim |title=''Camassia quamash'' - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Camassia_quamash |website=Flora of North America |access-date=4 July 2024 |date=5 November 2020}}</ref>
It is a [[monocot]] that has grasslike leaves, as typical of that group, that emerge from a persistent [[bulb]].<ref name="SagebrushCo">{{Cite book|last=Taylor|first=Ronald J.|title=Sagebrush Country: A Wildflower Sanctuary|publisher=Mountain Press Pub. Co|year=1994|isbn=0-87842-280-3|edition=rev.|location=Missoula, MT|pages=80|language=en|oclc=25708726|orig-year=1992}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Common Camas Camassia quamash |url=https://calscape.org/Camassia-quamash-(Common-Camas) |website=Calscape |publisher=California Native Plant Society |access-date=20 June 2024}}</ref> The bulb is of moderate size, {{convert|1 to 5|cm|in|frac=4|sp=us}} in diameter. The bulbs do not frequently cluster together and their surface is black while the interior is white with layers like that of an onion.<ref name="FNA" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Williams |first1=Kim |title=Eating Wild Plants |date=1977 |publisher=Mountain Press Publishing Company |location=Missoula, Montana |isbn=978-0-87842-065-0 |pages=64–66 |url=https://archive.org/details/eatingwildplants00will/page/64 |access-date=5 July 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

The leaves very rarely number more than nine on a plant and range in length from {{cvt|10 to 60|cm|in|0}}. In comparison to their length they are quite narrow, {{convert|4 to 20|mm|in}} in width. The upper surface of the leaves may or may not have a pale, waxy coating depending on the variety.<ref name="FNA" /> All the leaves spring from the base of the plant and the sturdy stem is leafless.<ref name="RMtnWildflowers">{{cite book |last1=Pavia |first1=Jerry |title=Rocky Mountain Wildflowers : Photos, Descriptions, and Early Explorer Insights |date=2003 |publisher=Fulcrum Publishing |location=Golden, Colorado |isbn=978-1-55591-364-9 |pages=164–165 |url=https://archive.org/details/rockymountainwil00pavi/page/164 |language=en}}</ref>

The flowering stems in wild or cultivated plants can be up to {{convert|80|cm|ft|sp=us}}, but may be as short as {{cvt|20|cm|in|0}}.<ref name="FNA" /><ref name="Brickell">{{cite book |editor1-last=Brickell |editor1-first=Christopher |title=New Encyclopedia of Plants and Flowers |date=1999 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley |location=London |isbn=978-0-7513-0800-6 |page=513 |edition=Third |url=https://archive.org/details/newencyclopediao0000unse_m3o8/page/513 |access-date=4 July 2024 |language=en}}</ref> As the [[inflorescence]] does not have branches it is a [[raceme]].<ref name="RMtnWildflowers" />

The pale blue to deep blue [[flower]]s appear in late spring to early summer (May to June in their native habitat). Each of the radially symmetrical, star-shaped flowers<ref name="SNW" /> has six [[tepal]]s, about {{Cvt|2.5|cm|frac=4}} across, and six stamens.<ref name="SagebrushCo" />

The leaves and bulbs of the plant are similar to the toxic white-flowered [[meadow death-camas]], a plant that is not in ''Camassia'', but part of the death-camas genus (''[[Toxicoscordion]]'') and grows in the same areas.<ref name="Pojar & MacKinnon" /><ref name="SNW" />

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Camassia quamash 6374.JPG|thumb|''C. quamash'' subsp. ''maxima'']]

There are eight [[subspecies]];<ref>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/qsearch.do World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref>
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''azurea'' – small camas
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''breviflora'' – small camas
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''intermedia'' – small camas
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''linearis'' – small camas
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''maxima'' – small camas
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''quamash'' – common camas
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''utahensis'' – Utah small camas
*''Camassia quamash'' subsp. ''walpolei'' – Walpole's small camas

===Etymology===
The [[genus]] name comes from the [[Nez Perce language|Nez Perce Indian]] name for this plant, and means "sweet".<ref name="SNW">{{cite book |last1=Wiese |first1=Karen |title=Sierra Nevada Wildflowers : a Field guide to Common Wildflowers and Shrubs of the Sierra Nevada, Including Yosemite, Sequoia, and Kings Canyon National Parks |date=2013 |publisher=FalconGuides |location=Guilford, Connecticut |isbn=978-0-7627-8034-1 |pages=22, 170 |edition=Second |url=https://archive.org/details/sierranevadawild0000wies/page/22 |access-date=4 July 2024 |language=en}}</ref> ''Qém'es'', a term for the plant's [[bulb]], which was gathered and used as a food source by tribes in the [[Pacific Northwest]], and were an important food source for the [[Lewis and Clark Expedition]] (1804–1806).<ref name=SNW/> The bulbs are or were harvested and pit-roasted or boiled by women of the [[Nez Perce]],<ref name="SagebrushCo" /> [[Cree]], and [[Blackfoot]] tribes.

==Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Camassia quamash 6394.JPG|thumb|''C. quamash'' subsp. ''maxima'', [[Skagit County, Washington]]]]

The species is [[Native plant|native]] to western [[North America]] in large areas of southern [[Canada]] and the northwestern [[United States]], from [[British Columbia]] and [[Alberta]] to [[California]] and east from [[Washington (state)|Washington]] state to [[Montana]] and [[Wyoming]].

Though the once-immense spreads of camas lands have diminished because of modern developments and agriculture, numerous [[camas prairie]]s and [[marsh]]es may still be seen today. In the [[Great Basin]], expanded settlement by whites accompanied by turning cattle and hogs onto camas prairies greatly diminished food available to native tribes and increased tension between Native Americans and settlers and travelers.<ref>''The Shoshoni Frontier and the Bear River Massacre'', Brigham D. Madsen, foreword by Charles S. Peterson, University of Utah Press (1985, paperback 1995), trade paperback, 286 pages, {{ISBN|0-87480-494-9}}</ref> Both the [[Bannock War|Bannock]] and [[Nez Perce War]]s began after Nez Perce became incensed at the failure of the US government to uphold [[Treaty Clause|treaties]], and at [[Settler colonialism|settlers]] who plowed up their camas prairies, which they depended on for subsistence.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clute|first=Willard Nelson|title=The American botanist, devoted to economic and ecological botany, Volumes 11-15|year=1907|publisher=W.N. Clute & co.|page=98}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Mathews|first=Daniel|title=Cascade-Olympic Natural History: a trailside reference|year=1999|publisher=Raven Editions|page=168|isbn=978-0-9620782-1-7}}</ref><ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120730075855/http://www.essortment.com/bannockwarindi_rfjo.htm|title=Native American History: The Bannock War}} Retrieved 1 March 2008.</ref><ref>Brimlow, George Francis. ''Harney County and Its Range Land'', 1951, Binfords & Mort, Portland, Oregon, p. 102ff.</ref>

==Cultivation==
This bulb flower naturalizes well in gardens. The bulb grows best in well-drained soil high in [[humus]]. It will grow in lightly shaded [[forest]] areas and on rocky [[outcrop]]s as well as in open [[meadow]]s or [[prairie]]s. Additionally, it is found growing alongside [[stream]]s and [[river]]s. The plants may be [[Division (horticulture)|divided]] in autumn after the leaves have withered. Additionally, the plant spreads by [[seed]] rather than by [[Stolon|runners]].{{cn|date=July 2025}}

In the [[Pacific Northwest]], [[Lekwungen]] peoples and others have cultivated kwetlal bulbs since precolonial times. Kwetlal has been promoted as a good replacement for invasive species for environmental and cultural restoration.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sidaway |first1=Kori |title=Call it kwetlal, not camas: How to decolonize your garden |url=https://cheknews.ca/call-it-kwetlal-not-camas-how-to-decolonize-your-garden-1152676/ |access-date=18 July 2025 |work=[[CHEK News]] |date=17 May 2023 |language=en-CA}}</ref>

==Uses==
Camas is grown as an [[ornamental plant]]. Even in the wild, large numbers of camas can color an entire meadow blue-violet.

===Food===
The bulbs of this ''Camassia'' species are edible and nutritious when roasted or boiled,<ref>{{cite book |last=Lyons |first=C. P. |author-link=C. P. Lyons |title=Trees, Shrubs and Flowers to Know in Washington |date=1956 |publisher=J. M. Dent & Sons |location=Canada |page=196 |edition=1st}}</ref> but are easily confused with those of the [[deathcamas]]. Though the white deathcamas flowers are very different, the bulbs are difficult to distinguish.<ref name="Pojar & MacKinnon">{{cite book |editor1-last=Pojar |editor1-first=Jim |editor2-last=MacKinnon |editor2-first=Andy |title=Plants of the Pacific Northwest Coast : Washington, Oregon, British Columbia & Alaska |date=2004 |publisher=Lone Pine Publishing |location=Vancouver, British Columbia |isbn=978-1-55105-530-5 |pages=108–109 |edition=Revised |url=https://archive.org/details/plantsofpacificn0000unse/page/108 |access-date=4 July 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="SNW" />

Camas has been a [[food]] source for many [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|native peoples]] in the western United States and Canada. After being harvested in the autumn, once the flowers have withered, the bulbs are pit-roasted or boiled.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Freedman|first=Robert Louis|title=Native North American Food Preparation Techniques|journal=Boletín Bibliográfico de Antropología Americana (1973-1979)|publisher=Pan American Institute of Geography and History|volume=38|issue=47 |page=131|date=1976|jstor=43996285|language=en}}, s.v. Camas Salish</ref> The latter produced a syrup.<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=Stephen |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf |location=New York |isbn=0-394-73127-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/595 595] |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/595 }}</ref> A [[Earth oven|pit-cooked]] camas bulb looks and tastes something like baked [[sweet potato]], but sweeter, and with more crystalline [[Natural fiber|fibers]] due to the presence of [[inulin]] in the bulbs—an [[oligosaccharide]] responsible for the copious [[flatulence]] caused by excessive consumption  of undercooked bulbs. Bulbs can also be dried and pounded into [[flour]], which can be used for baking or as a thickener.<ref name="pieroni">{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Pieroni |first1=Andrea |author-link=Andrea Pieroni (ethnobotanist) |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=34 |isbn=0415927463}}</ref><ref>Doherty, Craig A.;Doherty, Katherine M. Plateau Indians, Infobase Publishing, 2008, p. 42, {{ISBN|978-0-8160-5971-3}}</ref> Native American tribes who have eaten camas include the Nez Perce, Cree, [[Coast Salish peoples|Coast Salish]], [[Lummi people|Lummi]], and Blackfoot tribes, among many others. Camas bulbs contributed to the survival of members of the [[Lewis and Clark Expedition]] (1804–06).

Camas bulbs (and [[Bannock (Indigenous American food)|bannock]] made from them) are listed in the [[Ark of Taste]].<ref>[https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/camas-bulbs/ Camas Bulbs], [[Ark of Taste]], Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity</ref><ref>[https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/traditional-bannock/ Quamash Bannock], [[Ark of Taste]], Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity</ref>
